newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Northern Ireland Loyalist threatens truce breach.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland Loyalist threatens truce breach.

text.p: A member of Northern Ireland's pro-British guerrillas said in remarks published on Saturday his organisation would end a two-year-old truce if its IRA foes killed anyone in its war to end British rule of the province.

A "senior Loyalist paramilitary source" told the Irish Times the outlawed Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) would launch a campaign against their pro-Irish nationalist adversaries if the IRA killed anyone in its latest campaign.

His comments increased fears that Loyalists, who want the province to remain British, might abandon their two-year-long truce because of IRA violence and return to the tit-for-tat war which killed 3,200 people in 27 years.

The UFF is one of two Loyalist groups which have stuck by a ceasefire called in October 1994 when it matched a ceasefire declared and later abandoned by its ideological rival, the Irish Republican Army.
The source told the newspaper that if a huge IRA bomb which the guerrillas abandoned at Belfast Castle on New Year's Eve had killed anyone, the UFF "would be back, big time."

The IRA abandoned the bomb in a stolen van because tight security around the provincial capital prevented the guerrillas from placing it at its intended target, usually a British army or local police installation.

Police said the 1,000 lb (480 kg) device was assembled with the aim of "mass murder" and said it appeared to herald the launch of a New Year's campaign by the IRA, which abandoned its own ceasefire in February last year.

The UFF source declined to comment on whether the organisation carried out two booby-trap car bomb attacks on leading members of the Irish republican movement in Londonderry and Belfast in the past two weeks. A Catholic man was seriously injured by one of the devices.
The Combined Loyalist Military Command, the umbrella group for the two organisations, has not issued any statement about whether or not it will abide by its 26-month truce.

The ceasefire enabled political groups close to the Loylalist guerrillas to win seats at Northern Ireland peace talks from which Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, is excluded because of its return to violence in February 1994/
Britain and Ireland, co-sponsors of the slow-moving negotiations, say only parties which are committed the exclusive use of peaceful means to further their political ends can take part in the talks.
The IRA bombed Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters at Lisburn, near Belfast, last October, killing one soldier and injuring 30 in its most violent attack for months.
Security sources say troops and police are on alert against further outrages across the province and have urged people to be vigilant.
